video_title: David Rosenberg: "The Fed Just Made a Policy Mistake"
gist: Recorded minutes after a unanimous 25bp Fed rate hike, David Rosenberg argues the Fed is tightening into an oil-driven cost shock rather than demand- or wage-led inflation, calls it a policy mistake that sets up more mistakes next year, and says the Fed's talk of 'relative prices' is code for engineering a recession to offset ~40% higher energy costs. He frames this FOMC as a potential 'seminal event' and trigger for a major equity correction given 3-sigma valuations, record index concentration, cross-sector correlation to the AI trade, and early credit cracks (private credit defaults above 6%, Oracle CDS blowout) — and says he has raised 10% cash and will likely double it.

themes.theme: Hawkish hike into a supply shock

insights.claim: David Rosenberg says the Fed's 25bp hike was a policy mistake and that the committee is setting up a series of further policy mistakes over the next year, because it is tightening into an energy-driven cost shock rather than demand-led inflation.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: If the tightening path is a mistake, the pain shows up first in rate-sensitive and leveraged equity exposure, and later in a forced dovish reversal that steepens the curve.
insights.quote: I think the Fed made a policy mistake. I think that they are now setting us up for a series of poly mistakes in the next year.

insights.claim: The genuine surprise was not the hike itself — priced near 90-93% — but that the dovish FOMC members who dissented against a no-change decision only six weeks earlier capitulated and signaled willingness to hike again in October or December.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: A committee that flipped from three dissents to unanimity in six weeks has a much lower bar for further hikes than the dot plot implies.

insights.claim: Rosenberg expects the Fed to avoid moving before the midterm election, making December the live meeting, while futures had gone to roughly 50/50 on October and are now pricing three hikes next year versus the Fed's own dot plot of about one.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: The market is already positioned more hawkish than the Fed; a December-only path means front-end rates stay elevated into year-end with little relief priced out.
insights.quote: now they're pricing in three hikes for next year

insights.claim: The bond market rejected the idea that a hike would calm the long end: the 2-year note rose about 10bp from pre-statement levels, the 10-year gave up its rally, and the long bond yield was down only about two basis points after having been down five.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Directly falsifies the popular 'hawkish hike bull-steepens/rallies the back end' trade — duration did not get the credibility bid.
insights.quote: The two-year note, I think from pre press statement is up 10 basis points.

insights.claim: Rosenberg argues the Fed cannot credibly call the labor market fully employed when average hourly earnings growth has decelerated to about 3% year-over-year, the weakest in five years — in a genuinely tight market wages would be accelerating at least in line with prices.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Decelerating nominal wages remove the wage-price spiral justification for hiking and argue the inflation impulse is not self-sustaining.
insights.quote: how can you say with a straight face that the labor market is tight or that we're full employment when nominal wage growth is slowing down?

insights.claim: Beneath a 4.1% unemployment rate, the hiring rate and voluntary quits rate are both falling into a no-hire/no-fire backdrop that has left employment growth near zero year-over-year on both the payroll and household surveys.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: A zero-job-growth economy with a low unemployment rate is one labor-supply shock away from rising unemployment — watch quits and hires, not the headline rate.

insights.claim: With unit labor costs running at just 1.4% year-over-year and roughly 90% of the past year's economic growth coming from productivity, Rosenberg says there is no coherent structural or cyclical inflation case to be made from the labor market.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Labor cost is the transmission channel for durable inflation; at 1.4% the Fed is fighting a price level shift, not an inflation process.
insights.quote: labor costs up 1.4% year-over-year

insights.claim: Rosenberg classifies the current inflation as a supply-side cost shock — energy costs up roughly 40% — that functions economically like a tax increase, unlike the unionized COLA-protected 1970s or the stimulus-and-jobless-benefit demand surge of 2021-2023.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Cost-shock inflation self-corrects through demand destruction; tightening into it converts a one-off price rise into a recession.
insights.quote: This is not a demandled inflation. This is not wageled inflation. This is a cost shock. This is like tightening into a de facto tax increase.

insights.claim: Rosenberg reads the Fed Chair's emphasis on 'relative prices' as explicit code for deliberately deflating the non-energy price system to offset the oil shock and hit the 2% target — an outcome only achievable by causing a recession.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: If the reaction function is 'offset energy by crushing everything else,' the terminal rate is whatever breaks demand — a case for owning duration and defensives, not cyclicals.
insights.quote: I'm gonna have to deflate wide swas of the rest of the economy and you'll only do that by causing a recession.

insights.claim: Rosenberg's historical benchmark is that Bernanke did not raise rates when oil went from $50 to $150 in 2008 with inflation at 6% — double today's rate — and inflation collapsed to -2% a year later, and Greenspan cut five times during the Gulf War oil spike from $15 to $40.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Precedent says central banks look through oil shocks; deviating from that precedent raises the odds of an overshoot and a sharp later easing cycle.
insights.quote: Inflation was 6% when oil prices got to $150 a barrel in the summer of 2008. Did Bernanki raise rates?

insights.claim: The Dallas Fed trimmed mean, which strips idiosyncratic noise and was the Fed Chair's own previously favored gauge, sits at 2.3% versus 2.7% a year ago — evidence that underlying inflation is decelerating and only 30bp above target.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: The cleanest core measure undercuts the hawkish case; a rebound or continued fall in this series is the tell on whether the Fed has to back off.
insights.quote: Your own former favorite indicator is a 2.3.

insights.claim: Rosenberg says there is no evidence of the energy shock passing through to the broad price system — just as tariffs raised prices without feeding into wages or general inflation — and that demand destruction is already visible at the margin in energy, which is why oil has not retested its earlier highs.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: If pass-through never arrives, the hiking cycle is built on a forecast that does not materialize — a setup for a hard policy reversal.

themes.theme: Two props holding up the economy

insights.claim: Rosenberg says the economy rests on only two props: the AI data-center construction and capex boom, with data construction spending up around 70% while the rest of business capex is flat year-over-year and other commercial construction is down about 7%.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Ex-AI, US investment is already contracting — any slowdown in data-center spend removes one of the two legs under GDP.

insights.claim: The second prop is the equity wealth effect: consumer spending is growing above 2% year-over-year while real disposable income growth is near zero, with the household net-worth-to-income ratio at a record high and roughly 90% correlated with consumer spending.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Spending is now as sensitive to asset prices as to income, so an equity drawdown transmits directly into consumption — the market is the economy.
insights.quote: Do you know that this is a we're a financial asset economy? We are a financial asset economy.

insights.claim: Even with the technology capex boom, year-over-year industrial production growth is only about 1%, which Rosenberg offers as evidence the economy is neither robust nor resilient despite the Fed's language.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: A 1% IP trend is inconsistent with a boom narrative and argues against cyclical/industrial exposure priced for acceleration.
insights.quote: the year-over-year trend industrial production is 1%

insights.claim: Rosenberg invokes Jeremy Grantham's two-sigma definition of a price bubble and notes both the Buffett indicator and a CAPE near 40 are three-standard-deviation events, with the Buffett indicator possibly at an all-time high and overall valuations the second highest on record.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Three-sigma valuation with rising discount rates is the setup for multiple compression regardless of earnings delivery.
insights.quote: the bubble is not in the technology. The bubble is in our behavior, it's in valuations.

insights.claim: Index concentration is more extreme than at the 2000 peak: the top 10 names are over 40% of market cap versus under 30% then, and eight of the top 10 are technology companies versus five of 10 in 1999-2000.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Passive index exposure is now a concentrated tech bet — diversification via the S&P is largely illusory.
insights.quote: Over 40% t top 10 market cap stocks. It was less than 30% at the peak in the late 1990s.

insights.claim: Unlike the late 1990s when only media and telecom were correlated with technology, today every S&P sector except healthcare and staples is highly correlated to the tech/AI trade — utilities, energy, financials and industrials included, with Caterpillar acting as the non-tech AI proxy.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: An explicit sector-rotation map: healthcare and staples are the only genuine hiding places if the AI trade unwinds.
insights.quote: The only two sectors that don't have a correlation with this tech trade, which is healthcare and staples.

insights.claim: Positioning is universally long: 72% of the household financial balance sheet is in equities versus only 7% in bonds, and equity mutual funds are sitting on about 1% cash — nobody has rebalanced or taken profits.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: With no dry powder in funds and record household equity weight, there is no marginal buyer to cushion a drawdown.
insights.quote: 72% of the household financial balance sheet is in equities. Nobody's rebalanced. Nobody's taken profits. By the way, only 7% is in bonds.

insights.claim: Rosenberg says the credit market always leads the stock market and points to Fitch reporting the private credit default rate rising above 6% for the first time as the current warning signal.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Private credit default rates are the leading indicator to monitor; a 6%+ print argues for de-risking equity beta before spreads gap.
insights.quote: the default rate in uh in private credit just went above 6% for the first time

insights.claim: Rosenberg identifies Oracle as the poster child of AI-financing stress, citing its blown-out CDS spreads, after hyperscalers proved unable to self-fund their capex binge and began issuing debt in size at the long end in multiple currencies with implications for their credit ratings.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Oracle CDS is a tradable early-warning gauge on whether the AI buildout can keep financing itself at higher rates.
insights.quote: I think Oracle is the poster child. That'll be something else about how their CDS spreads have blown out.

insights.claim: The semiconductor index is already down more than 20% from its recent all-time highs into an official bear market, which matters because Katie Stockton told Rosenberg her favorite leading indicator for the broad market is the semiconductors as the best cyclical signal.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: A semis bear market has historically led the broad tape — treat SOX weakness as a broad-market sell signal rather than sector noise.
insights.quote: the semiconductors are the best cyclical indicator for the rest of the market

insights.claim: Dan Nathan flags that AI risk now sits in novel financing structures — GPUs pledged as collateral for debt, plus equity offerings and private credit — with the exposure held by insurance companies, pension funds and sovereign wealth funds who, if valuations fall, will be forced to sell whatever is liquid, with OpenAI testing private markets at a $1.5 trillion valuation versus roughly $250 billion at the start of 2025.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Illiquid private AI marks mean the selling pressure lands first on liquid large-cap tech — the supposed 'defensive' MAG 7 rotation is the exit door.
insights.quote: They're going to sell what's liquid

insights.claim: Rosenberg raised 10% cash in his model portfolio in the week before this Fed meeting and said the hawkish outcome means he will probably double that cash position and de-risk further.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: A live, dated allocation change — roughly 20% cash — from a manager acting on his own macro call rather than commentating on it.
insights.quote: I just raised 10% cash last week in that model portfolio. I'm going to probably double up on that.

insights.claim: Rosenberg suggests the S&P 500 peak on August 13th, with the 10-year note around 4.75% that day, may in hindsight mark the top, and that this FOMC meeting could be the seminal trigger point for a real, large equity correction.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Gives a specific date and yield level to benchmark against — a break of the August 13th high would invalidate the call.
insights.quote: we might look back at this as as the trigger point for a real big correction in the stock market
